title: How finance offers work
summary: How loan, card, insurance and banking offers pay, why approval rates and lead quality decide your profit, and how to compare CPL with CPA on approval or funding. You finish able to read a finance offer, run the economics and refuse the offers that harm people.

lessons.title: The finance lead-gen map: products, players and money
objectives: By the end you can name the five main finance product groups and what each one pays for.
You can draw the path from an ad to a payout and say who decides each step.
You can work out what one click is worth from a payout and a funded rate.
You can explain why finance is regulated and why that changes how you buy traffic.

steps.h: Why finance pays well, and why it is watched
steps.p: Lenders, card issuers, insurers and banks pay affiliates because a good customer is worth a lot to them over months or years. The same fact makes finance regulated: you are helping a person take on debt, buy cover or hand over financial data. High payouts and high responsibility come together.
steps.more: A credit card customer may pay fees and interest for years. An insurance customer pays a premium every month. A bank customer may hold savings and take loans later. The advertiser can afford a large payout because they expect to earn more than that over the life of the account. That same long relationship is why regulators care: a bad loan or the wrong policy follows a person for years. In this school you learn to make money in finance by sending people who should get the product, telling them the true cost, and collecting data only with their clear consent. That is also the approach that survives platform reviews and network audits.

d.b: You are selling access to money
d.s: The payout is high because the customer is valuable and the product can hurt people.

steps.say: Let's start with why finance pays well. Lenders, card issuers, insurers and banks pay affiliates because a good customer is worth a lot to them, over months or years. A card customer may pay fees for years. An insurance customer pays every month. But that same fact makes finance regulated. You're helping a person take on debt, buy cover, or hand over financial data. As the slide says, you're selling access to money. High payouts and high responsibility come together.

steps.h: The players between an ad and a payout
steps.p: Every finance campaign has the same skeleton. You bring the person. A network or aggregator routes the lead. The lender, issuer or insurer decides. A postback tells you what happened. Only some of those decisions are in your hands.
steps.more: Underwriting is the advertiser's check of whether to approve someone: identity, income, credit history and affordability. You do not control it, but your traffic strongly affects it. If your ad attracts people who meet the lender's criteria, more get approved. If it attracts people who cannot qualify, approvals fall and your payout per lead falls with them. The network sits in the middle: it holds the offer terms, checks lead quality, passes status back and pays you.
steps.say: Every finance campaign has the same skeleton, and this map shows it. Follow it along. The applicant sees your ad and clicks to a form or comparison page. The lead goes to a network or aggregator, which routes it to the lender, issuer or insurer. They make the underwriting decision, checking identity, income, credit and affordability. A postback reports the status, and you get paid if it's a paid event. You don't control underwriting, but your traffic strongly affects it.

steps.h: The five product groups you will meet
steps.p: Each group has a different buyer, a different paid event and a different kind of harm if done badly. Know which one you are promoting before you write copy.
steps.more: Short-term, high-cost loans (often called payday loans) sit inside the first group but carry the highest risk of harm and the strictest rules. Some platforms and countries restrict or ban advertising them at the time of writing. We cover how to judge them in the compliance module. As a first offer, avoid them.
d: Personal and digital loans|Instalment or short-term credit; paid on approval or funding
Credit cards and BNPL|Revolving credit; paid on approval, sometimes activation
Insurance|Car, health, life, device; paid per quote lead or bought policy
Banking and savings|Accounts and apps; paid on open or first deposit
Lead generation|You collect consented data; paid per valid lead
steps.say: Here are the five product groups you'll meet. Personal and digital loans, paid on approval or funding. Credit cards and B N P L, buy now pay later, paid on approval, sometimes activation. Insurance, paid per quote lead or bought policy. Banking and savings, paid when an account opens or gets a first deposit. And lead generation, where you collect consented data and get paid per valid lead. Short-term, high cost loans carry the highest risk of harm and the strictest rules, so as a first offer, avoid them.

steps.h: What each product usually pays for
steps.p: Rough guide, varies by geo, network and advertiser. Always read the offer's own definition of the paid event, because two offers with the same name can pay on very different events.
steps.say: This table shows what each product usually pays for, and how long it takes to confirm. Read across. A personal loan pays on an approved or funded loan, in days to weeks. A credit card, on an approved card. Insurance, on a quote lead or bought policy, in hours to weeks. A bank account, when it's opened. And lead gen, C P L, cost per lead, on a valid, consented lead. This is a rough guide that varies by geo and network. Always read the offer's own definition, because two offers with the same name can pay on very different events.

steps.h: The life of one finance lead
steps.p: Most of the value is decided after the click, often days later. That delay is the biggest difference between finance and a simple e-commerce sale, and it shapes your budget, your kill rules and your cash flow.
steps.say: Here's the life of one finance lead. Click. Form submitted. Lead validated. Application. Approval. And finally, funding and payout. Notice how most of the value is decided after the click, often days later. That delay is the biggest difference between finance and a simple e-commerce sale. It shapes your budget, your kill rules and your cash flow.

steps.h: Worked example: 1,000 clicks to funded loans
steps.p: Example, illustrative numbers. Of 1,000 clicks, 90 submit the form, 72 pass validation, 22 are approved and 15 are funded. At $60 per funded loan that is $900. If the clicks cost $0.50 each, spend is $500 and profit is $400 before any later reversals.
steps.more: Check the maths. 15 x $60 = $900 revenue. 1,000 x $0.50 = $500 spend. $900 minus $500 = $400. Now notice how fragile it is: if only 8 loans had been funded instead of 15, revenue would be $480 and you would lose $20. A small change in the funded rate swings the whole result. That is why lead quality and approval rate get whole lessons in this module, and why you never judge a finance campaign on clicks or form submits alone.
steps.say: Let's follow one thousand clicks, with illustrative numbers. Ninety submit the form. Seventy two pass validation. Twenty two are approved. And fifteen are funded. At sixty dollars per funded loan, that's nine hundred dollars. If clicks cost fifty cents each, spend is five hundred, and profit is four hundred, before any reversals. But notice how fragile this is. If only eight loans were funded, revenue would be four eighty, and you'd lose twenty dollars. That's why you never judge finance on clicks or form submits alone.

steps.h: What one click is worth
steps.p: Turn any payout into a value per click. Multiply the payout by the share of clicks that reach the paid event. This is the ceiling on what you can pay per click and still break even.
steps.more: Example. 15 funded from 1,000 clicks is 1.5%. $60 x 0.015 = $0.90. That is break-even per click. You want to pay well under it, because you need a margin and because the funded rate in your first week is only an estimate. If you keep a 30% margin, your ceiling is $0.63 per click.
steps.say: Here's how to turn any payout into a value per click. Read the sum on screen. Sixty dollars per funded loan, times one point five percent of clicks reaching funding, equals ninety cents per click. That's your break-even ceiling. You want to pay well under it, because you need a margin, and your first week's funded rate is only an estimate. With a thirty percent margin, your ceiling is sixty three cents per click.

steps.h: What a network report usually shows
steps.p: Finance networks report each lead by status. Learn to read pending as unknown, not as zero and not as approved. Screen is an illustrative mock-up; real dashboards differ.

steps.p: You are not paid for clicks or forms. You are paid when a lender says yes and the person goes ahead. So your job is to reach people who need the product and can qualify, and to tell them the truth about cost so the ones who apply are ready.

lessons.title: Payout models: CPL, CPA on approval, CPA on funding
objectives: By the end you can explain CPL, CPA on approval, CPA on funding, pay per call and tiered pricing.
You can say who carries the approval risk in each model.
You can convert any payout into a value per submitted lead and compare offers fairly.
You can pick a model that fits your cash flow.

steps.h: Why the payout model matters as much as the payout
steps.p: Two offers can show $4 and $40 and the $4 one can be the better deal. What matters is the payout times the share of leads that reach the paid event, how long you wait for it, and who carries the risk that the lender says no.

d.b: Compare value per lead, not payout
d.s: A big number on a hard event can be worth less than a small number on an easy one.

steps.say: Here's a surprising idea. Two offers can show four dollars and forty dollars, and the four dollar one can be the better deal. What matters is the payout times the share of leads that reach the paid event, how long you wait for it, and who carries the risk that the lender says no. As the slide says: compare value per lead, not payout. A big number on a hard event can be worth less than a small number on an easy one.

steps.h: The payout models in finance
steps.p: These are the models you will see on finance offer pages. Many offers mix two of them. Always read the exact wording, because networks use the same labels for different events.
steps.more: SOI (single opt-in) means one form submit counts. DOI (double opt-in) means the person also confirms, for example by an SMS code or email link. A ping tree is a system where a lead is offered to several buyers in order of price until one accepts it. RevShare, a share of the advertiser's income from the customer, is rare in finance; if you see it, ask how the income is measured and reported.
d: CPL|Paid per valid lead; the advertiser carries approval risk
CPA on approval|Paid when the lender approves
CPA on funding|Paid when money is paid out or the card is issued
Pay per call|Paid for a qualified call over a minimum length
Tiered or dynamic|Price depends on lead data or buyer bids
Hybrid|A small CPL plus a CPA on approval
steps.say: These are the payout models you'll see on finance offer pages. C P L, cost per lead: paid per valid lead, so the advertiser carries the approval risk. C P A, cost per acquisition, on approval: paid when the lender approves. C P A on funding: paid when money is paid out or the card is issued. Pay per call: paid for a qualified call over a minimum length. Tiered or dynamic: the price depends on lead data or buyer bids. And hybrid: a small C P L plus a C P A on approval. Many offers mix two, so always read the exact wording.

steps.h: Who carries the risk in each model
steps.p: The further down the funnel you are paid, the more of the advertiser's risk you carry. In return, the payout is bigger. Rough guide; read each offer.
steps.say: This table shows who carries the risk in each model. Read across. On C P L, you're paid when the lead is valid, and you carry the risk of scrubs and returns. On C P A on approval, you carry the approval rate. On C P A on funding, both approval and drop-off. On pay per call, call quality. And hybrid splits the risk. The rule: the further down the funnel you're paid, the more of the advertiser's risk you carry, and in return, the payout is bigger.

steps.h: Turn every payout into value per lead
steps.p: This one formula lets you compare any two finance offers on the same footing. Use the rate from the offer's own history for similar traffic, then replace it with your own data as soon as you have it.
steps.say: This one formula lets you compare any two finance offers on the same footing. Read the sum on screen: payout, times the share of leads reaching the paid event, equals value per lead. Start with the rate from the offer's own history for similar traffic. Then replace it with your own data as soon as you have it.

steps.h: Worked example: the same 100 leads, three models
steps.p: Example, illustrative rates. 100 submitted leads go to three offers. The CPL looks smallest but is close to the others, and it pays fastest. The CPA offers win only if their rates hold up for your traffic.
steps.more: Check the maths. CPL: 100 leads minus 15% scrubbed is 85 accepted, x $4 = $340. Approval: 18 approved x $25 = $450. Funding: 11 funded x $40 = $440. Hybrid: 100 x $1 = $100 plus 15 approvals x $20 = $300, total $400. The CPA on approval pays most here, but it depends on an 18% approval rate. If your traffic gets 12% instead, it earns 12 x $25 = $300, less than the CPL.
steps.say: Here are the same one hundred leads sent to different models, with illustrative rates. Read the table. C P L at four dollars with fifteen percent scrubbed: three forty, or three dollars forty per lead. C P A on approval at twenty five dollars, eighteen percent approved: four fifty. C P A on funding at forty, eleven percent funded: four forty. Hybrid: four hundred. The approval offer pays most here, but only if eighteen percent holds. At twelve percent, it earns three hundred, less than the C P L, which also pays fastest.

steps.h: Cash arrives at different speeds
steps.p: Example. Same weekly spend, two offers. The CPL confirms within days. The funding offer reaches a higher weekly revenue only after approvals mature, so the first weeks look bad and you need cash to wait.
steps.more: Example figures only. The funding line starts low because loans approved in week 1 are still being funded in weeks 2 and 3. If you judged it in week 1 you would kill a campaign that ends up earning about 30% more per week than the CPL. If you cannot afford to wait four weeks, the CPL may be the right choice even though it earns less at steady state.

steps.h: Lab: the most you can pay per lead
steps.p: Practise. Payout $40 per funded loan, 11% of leads get funded, and you want a 30% margin.
steps.more: Working: $40 x 11% = $4.40 break-even per lead. Keep 30%: $4.40 x 0.7 = $3.08. If your leads cost more than $3.08 you are below your margin target; above $4.40 you lose money.

steps.h: Pin down the paid event before you spend
steps.p: Ask the affiliate manager in writing before you spend. The answers go into your offer file, and they settle disputes later about what was promised. Ask for rates on traffic like yours, not the offer average. Chat is illustrative.

messages.text: For the KE personal loan offer, is the $40 paid on approval or on disbursement?
On disbursement. Status comes by postback, usually within 14 days.
What share of valid leads from social traffic were funded in the last 30 days?
Roughly 9 to 12 percent. It varies a lot by source.
Thanks. Please send the scrub rules and the payout definition by email so I can file them.

steps.say: Before you spend, pin down the paid event in writing. Look at this illustrative chat. You ask whether the forty dollars is paid on approval or disbursement. The manager says disbursement, usually within fourteen days. You ask what share of valid leads from social traffic were funded. Roughly nine to twelve percent, and it varies by source. Then you ask for the scrub rules and payout definition by email. Notice you asked for rates on traffic like yours, not the offer average. These answers go in your offer file and settle disputes later.

steps.h: Common mistakes with payout models
steps.p: Most losses in the first month come from comparing headline payouts or from not having the cash to wait for a CPA offer to mature.

a.title: Mistake
items: Picking the biggest payout on the list
Assuming approval and funding mean the same
Running CPA on funding with no cash buffer
Trusting a quoted rate as your own

b.title: Fix
items: Compare value per lead
Get the paid event in writing
Pick CPL until you can wait 30+ days
Replace quoted rates with your data fast

steps.say: Most losses in the first month come from comparing headline payouts, or from not having the cash to wait. Read across. Picking the biggest payout on the list: compare value per lead. Assuming approval and funding mean the same: get the paid event in writing. Running C P A on funding with no cash buffer: pick C P L until you can wait thirty days or more. And trusting a quoted rate as your own: replace quoted rates with your own data fast.

steps.h: Ping trees, pay per call and resold leads
steps.p: When a lead can be sold to several buyers, the person's consent must clearly cover that before the data moves. This is a legal and ethical line, not a technical detail, and networks will ask you to prove it.

d.text: Never sell or pass one person's data to more buyers than their consent covers. Ping trees and lead resale are restricted or under scrutiny in several markets; we are not certain of current rules in each geo, so ask your network and a local adviser.

steps.say: Now a legal and ethical line. When a lead can be sold to several buyers, through a ping tree, pay per call or resale, the person's consent must clearly cover that before the data moves. Networks will ask you to prove it. Look at the warning: never sell or pass one person's data to more buyers than their consent covers. Ping trees and lead resale are restricted or under scrutiny in several markets. We're not certain of the current rules in each geo, so ask your network and a local adviser.

steps.h: Worked example: a hybrid offer
steps.p: Hybrids pay a little on every valid lead and more on approval. They reduce your risk while you learn an offer, at the cost of a smaller total if your approval rate turns out high. Run the numbers both ways before you choose.

d.text: Example. 200 leads, hybrid $1 CPL + $20 per approval, 16% approved. 200 x $1 = $200. 32 x $20 = $640. Total $840, or $4.20 per lead. A pure $25 CPA would give 32 x $25 = $800.

steps.say: Here's a worked example of a hybrid offer. Two hundred leads, paying one dollar C P L plus twenty dollars per approval, with sixteen percent approved. Two hundred times one dollar is two hundred. Thirty two approvals times twenty is six forty. Total, eight hundred and forty dollars, or four twenty per lead. A pure twenty five dollar C P A would give eight hundred. So hybrids reduce your risk while you learn an offer, at the cost of a smaller total if your approval rate turns out high. Run the numbers both ways.

steps.p: Starting rules to adapt. Use them to choose between offers before spending, then revisit them after your first matured cohort, when your own rates replace the network's quoted ones.

steps.h: Why approval rate beats every other number
steps.p: In CPA finance offers, a small change in approval rate changes everything. Going from 15% to 10% approval cuts your revenue by a third with the same spend. Your targeting, angle and form design move this number more than most beginners expect.

d.b: Approval rate is your profit lever
d.s: Same leads, same cost: 15% vs 10% approval is a third less revenue.

steps.say: In C P A, cost per acquisition, finance offers, a small change in approval rate changes everything. Going from fifteen percent to ten percent approval cuts your revenue by a third, with the same spend. And your targeting, angle and form design move this number more than most beginners expect. As the slide says, approval rate is your profit lever.

steps.p: Example, illustrative. 500 submits, 430 valid, 300 complete the full application, 90 approved, 66 funded. Each step has its own rate and its own cause. Find the weakest step before you change anything.
steps.say: Here's an example funnel, from submits to funded. Follow it down. Five hundred form submits. Four hundred and thirty valid leads. Three hundred complete the full application. Ninety approved. Sixty six funded. Each step has its own rate, and its own cause. So before you change anything, find the weakest step.

steps.h: The stage rates from that funnel
steps.p: Example, from the funnel above. Write these five rates for every campaign. When profit moves, one of them moved, and you will know where to look.
steps.more: Rates rounded. Approval rate can be quoted per application or per lead; networks differ. Here 90 approvals from 430 valid leads is about 21% per valid lead, but 30% per completed application. Always ask which base a quoted rate uses, or you will plan with a number that is too high.
steps.say: These are the stage rates from that funnel. Read down. Valid rate, eighty six percent. Application rate, seventy percent. Approval rate, thirty percent of applications. Funding rate, seventy three percent. And submit to funded, thirteen point two percent. Write these five rates for every campaign. When profit moves, one of them moved. One warning: approval rate can be quoted per application or per lead. Here it's thirty percent per application, but about twenty one percent per valid lead. Always ask which base a quoted rate uses.

steps.h: From payout to max cost per lead
steps.p: Set your target cost per approval first, then turn it into a max cost per lead using your approval rate per lead. Example: $35 per approval, 18% of leads approved, 30% margin.
steps.more: Check: $35 x 0.18 = $6.30 break-even per lead. Keeping 30%: $6.30 x 0.7 = $4.41. Your target cost per approval is $35 x 0.7 = $24.50. Both lines describe the same plan: pay at most $4.41 per lead and you will land at or under $24.50 per approval if the 18% holds.
steps.say: Now turn your payout into a max cost per lead. In this example, the payout is thirty five dollars per approval, eighteen percent of leads are approved, and you want a thirty percent margin. Read the sum on screen. Thirty five times eighteen percent is six dollars thirty per lead, your break-even. Times point seven is four dollars forty one, your max C P L, cost per lead. Pay at most that, and you'll land at or under twenty four fifty per approval, if the eighteen percent holds.

steps.h: Approval lag: early numbers lie
steps.p: Example. A cohort of leads from one week, with $300 spent and 20 approvals in the end. On day 1 only a few are reported, so the cost per approval looks terrible. It settles only as approvals arrive.
steps.more: Example maths: final cost per approval is $300 / 20 = $15. On day 1, 10% of approvals (2) are reported, so it looks like $150. On day 7, 60% (12) gives $25. If your target were $24.50 you would have killed a campaign on day 7 that ends at $15. The lag differs by lender and product; ask the network how long it takes for most approvals to arrive, and measure it yourself.
steps.say: This curve shows why early numbers lie. It's one week's cohort, with three hundred dollars spent and twenty approvals in the end. Look at day one: only ten percent of approvals are reported, so cost per approval looks like one hundred and fifty dollars. By day seven, it looks like twenty five. And by day thirty, it settles at fifteen. If your target were twenty four fifty, you'd have killed this campaign on day seven. The lag differs by lender, so ask the network, and measure it yourself.

steps.h: Judge cohorts, not calendar days
steps.p: A cohort is the leads you generated in one period, such as one day or one week. Track each cohort's approvals until they mature. Compare matured cohorts with each other, never a fresh cohort with an old one.

d.b: Group leads by the day they came in
d.s: Read a cohort's approvals only after its approval window.

steps.say: So judge cohorts, not calendar days. A cohort is the leads you generated in one period, like one day or one week. Track each cohort's approvals until they mature. steps.h: Leading signals you can read early
steps.p: While approvals mature, these early numbers tell you if a cohort is on track. They are signals, not proof. Rough guide; set your own normal ranges from matured cohorts.

rows: Behind past cohorts at the same age

steps.say: While approvals mature, these early signals tell you if a cohort is on track. Read the table. Valid lead rate, same day: warning if it's well below your matured average. Application rate, one to three days: warning if falling week on week. Contact rate: warning if leads aren't answering. steps.h: Example: angle changes approval rate
steps.p: Example, illustrative numbers from a single test. Three angles, same offer and form. The urgency angle brought cheap leads with the lowest approval rate. The planning angles cost more per lead and earned more per lead.
steps.more: Example. At $35 per approval: the urgency angle at $1.80 per lead earns 0.09 x $35 = $3.15 per lead, profit $1.35. The purchase angle at $3.50 per lead earns 0.26 x $35 = $9.10, profit $5.60. The cheap lead was the expensive choice. Angles that speak to urgency also tend to reach people under the most financial pressure, which is a harm issue as well as a profit issue.
steps.say: Look at these three bars, from a single test with the same offer and form. Fast cash today brought cheap leads, but only nine percent approved. Spread a big cost got twenty two percent. The purchase angle at three fifty makes five sixty. The cheap lead was the expensive choice. And urgency angles also tend to reach people under the most financial pressure, which is a harm issue too.

steps.h: Common mistakes with approval data
steps.p: These mistakes come from impatience or from mixing up bases. Each one leads to killing good campaigns or scaling bad ones, and in finance you only find out weeks later, when the money is already spent.

a.title: Mistake
items: Killing on day-2 cost per approval
Mixing per-lead and per-application rates
Comparing a new cohort with a matured one
Chasing cheap leads with low approval

b.title: Fix
items: Wait for the approval window
Write the base next to every rate
Compare cohorts at the same age
Optimise value per lead, not CPL

steps.say: These mistakes come from impatience, or from mixing up bases. Read across. Killing on day two cost per approval: wait for the approval window. Mixing per lead and per application rates: write the base next to every rate. Comparing a new cohort with a matured one: compare cohorts at the same age. Chasing cheap leads with low approval: optimise value per lead, not C P L. In finance, you only find these mistakes weeks later, when the money's already spent.

steps.h: Never raise approvals by coaching applicants
steps.p: Approval rate rises honestly when you reach eligible people and explain the criteria clearly. It must never rise because someone was told what to type. That line is fraud, and lenders do check.

d.text: Never suggest that users overstate income, hide debts or use someone else's details. That is fraud, it harms the applicant, and lenders claw back payouts and report it. Pre-filling or editing applicant data is the same.

steps.h: Starting decision rules with approval lag
steps.p: Starting rules to adapt. T is your target cost per approval (payout x 0.7). The window is the number of days in which about 85% of approvals usually arrive for this offer.
steps.more: Example with T = $24.50. Early kill at $49 spend if fewer than 70% of leads are valid. Zero kill at $73.50 spend with no approvals after the window. Scale only when two matured cohorts each show cost per approval of $19.60 or less with at least five approvals. These are cautious on purpose: in finance, a bad scale decision is paid for weeks later.
d: Early kill: spend ≥ 2 x T and valid rate below 70%
Zero kill: spend ≥ 3 x T and 0 approvals after the window
Hold: any cohort younger than the window
Scale +20%: two matured cohorts at ≤ 0.8 x T, ≥ 5 approvals each
Pause: matured approval rate down by a third versus the last two
steps.say: Here are your starting decision rules. T is your target cost per approval, the payout times point seven. The window is the days in which about eighty five percent of approvals arrive. Early kill: spend of two times T or more and a valid rate below seventy percent. Zero kill: three times T spent and zero approvals after the window. Hold any cohort younger than the window. Scale by twenty percent when two matured cohorts are at point eight times T or better, with at least five approvals each. And pause if the matured approval rate drops by a third. These are cautious on purpose.

Approvals arrive late, so judge cohorts after their approval window.
Optimise value per lead, not the cheapest cost per lead.

lessons.title: Lead quality: real, eligible, contactable, consented
objectives: By the end you can name the four tests every finance lead must pass.
You can calculate net revenue after scrubs and returns.
You can spot duplicate, fake and incentivised leads in your own data.
You can apply exact pause rules when quality drops.

steps.h: Why lead quality is your income, not a detail
steps.p: Finance networks check every lead and pay only for the ones that pass. Bad leads are rejected now or clawed back later, and a pattern of them gets you removed. Quality decides how much of your spend turns into revenue.

d.b: You are paid for leads that pass checks
d.s: Everything else is spend with no revenue.

steps.say: Finance networks check every lead and pay only for the ones that pass. Bad leads are rejected now, or clawed back later. And a pattern of them gets you removed. So quality decides how much of your spend turns into revenue. As the slide says, you're paid for leads that pass checks. Everything else is spend with no revenue.

steps.h: The four tests of a good finance lead
steps.p: A lead must pass all four tests. Fail one and it is worth nothing to the buyer, or worse, it causes a complaint that reaches the network, the platform or a regulator.
d: Real|A real person, with correct name, phone and email
Eligible|Meets the product's basic criteria: age, geo, income
Contactable|Answers the call, SMS or email that follows
Consented|Agreed, clearly, to be contacted by this buyer
steps.say: A good finance lead must pass all four of these tests. Real: a real person, with a correct name, phone and email. Eligible: meets the product's basic criteria, like age, geo and income. Contactable: answers the call, S M S or email that follows. And consented: agreed, clearly, to be contacted by this buyer. Fail one and the lead is worth nothing to the buyer. Or worse, it causes a complaint that reaches the network, the platform, or a regulator.

steps.h: Why networks scrub leads
steps.p: Rough guide; each network has its own list. Ask for the scrub reasons per lead, because they tell you exactly what to fix, and fix the biggest reason first before touching anything else.
steps.say: Here's why networks scrub leads, with a likely cause and your fix. Duplicates: dedupe before sending. Invalid phones from typos or fakes: add a phone format check and an O T P, a one time code. Outside geo: tighten geo and check I P. Under age: add an age field. Ineligible: state the criteria upfront. No consent record: fix the form. Each network has its own list, so ask for the scrub reason per lead, and fix the biggest reason first.

steps.h: Worked example: net billable leads
steps.p: Example. 400 leads, 22% scrubbed, $3.50 per accepted lead. Revenue is far below what the raw lead count suggests, so always plan on accepted leads, never on form submits.
steps.more: Check: 400 x 0.78 = 312 accepted. 312 x $3.50 = $1,092. A buyer who planned on 400 x $3.50 = $1,400 overestimated revenue by $308.
steps.say: Here's a worked example of net billable leads. Four hundred leads, twenty two percent scrubbed, three dollars fifty per accepted lead. Read the sum on screen. Four hundred times seventy eight percent accepted, times three fifty, equals one thousand and ninety two dollars. A buyer who planned on all four hundred would expect fourteen hundred, and overestimate revenue by three hundred and eight dollars. So always plan on accepted leads, never on form submits.

steps.h: Worked example: the hidden cost of returns
steps.p: Example, illustrative. Spend $1,000 for 400 leads looks like a $2.50 CPL. After scrubs and later returns, the real margin is thin. Run this table for every CPL offer.
steps.more: A return is a lead the buyer accepted and later sends back, for example because the phone was disconnected or the person said they never applied. Networks often deduct returns from later payouts. 312 x 0.06 = 18.72, rounded to 19 returned leads. The campaign looked profitable at a $2.50 CPL against a $3.50 payout, but it made $25.50 on $1,000 of spend. One more point of scrub would have made it a loss.
steps.say: Now the hidden cost of returns. A return is a lead the buyer accepted and later sent back, for example a disconnected phone. Read down the table. One thousand dollars for four hundred leads looks like a two fifty C P L, cost per lead. Three hundred and twelve are accepted, so each accepted lead really costs three twenty one. Then six percent come back as returns, nineteen leads, leaving two hundred and ninety three paid. Revenue is one thousand and twenty five fifty. Profit, just twenty five dollars fifty. One more point of scrub would have made it a loss.

steps.h: Duplicates are paid once
steps.p: People often submit twice: once from the ad, once from a retargeting ad, or on two of your landers. The network pays once. Count duplicates before you count profit, and remove them before sending if your setup allows.

d.s: Dedupe on phone and email before you count leads.

steps.say: People often submit twice: once from the ad, once from a retargeting ad, or on two of your landers. But the network pays once. As the slide says: one person, one payout. So count duplicates before you count profit, and dedupe on phone and email before sending, if your setup allows.

steps.h: How to check your own leads for fraud
steps.p: Do this weekly on a sample of leads, or daily while testing a new source. You are looking for patterns no real group of people would produce. Screens are illustrative mock-ups.

steps.title: Sort by submit time
steps.text: Clusters of many leads in the same minute, at 3 a.m., are a warning.

steps.title: Look at fill time
steps.text: Real people take time to read and type. A median under about 15 seconds on a multi-field form needs a closer look.

blocks.value: Compare with your other sources. Example: 48 seconds.

steps.title: Check number patterns
steps.text: Sequential or repeated phone numbers and copied emails point to fake data.

steps.title: Pause and report
steps.text: Pause the source, tell the network what you found, and do not ask to be paid for those leads.

steps.say: Here's how to check your own leads for fraud. Do it weekly on a sample, or daily while testing a new source. Tap Next to follow each step. First, sort by submit time: many leads in the same minute, at three a m, is a warning. Second, look at fill time: a median under about fifteen seconds on a multi-field form needs a closer look. Here it's four seconds. Third, check number patterns: sequential phones and copied emails point to fake data. Finally, pause the source, tell the network what you found, and don't ask to be paid for those leads.

steps.h: Reading a network quality note
steps.p: Good managers tell you why leads failed. Act on it the same day and reply with what you changed, so they see you take quality seriously. That trust matters when caps are set. Chat is illustrative.

messages.text: Yesterday: 22% of your leads scrubbed. Most were invalid phones from one placement.
Thanks. Which placement, and can you share the lead IDs?
Excluded it today and added an SMS code check on the form. I will send tomorrow's numbers.

You ask which placement and for the lead I Ds. It's the in-app placement. Then you reply that you've excluded it today and added an S M S code check, and you'll send tomorrow's numbers. Act on it the same day and say what you changed. That trust matters when caps are set.

steps.h: Common mistakes that destroy lead quality
steps.p: Each of these can raise lead volume for a few days and then cost you the offer, the payouts already earned or the whole network relationship. Volume that fails checks is not volume.

a.title: Mistake
items: Paying users to fill forms
Buying traffic from unknown resellers
Letting every placement run
Removing fields to cut CPL

b.title: Fix
items: Only reach people who want the product
Use sources you control and can audit
Exclude placements that scrub high
Keep the fields the lender needs

steps.say: These mistakes can raise lead volume for a few days, then cost you the offer, your earned payouts, or the whole network relationship. Read across. Paying users to fill forms: only reach people who want the product. Buying traffic from unknown resellers: use sources you control and can audit. Letting every placement run: exclude placements that scrub high. Removing fields to cut C P L: keep the fields the lender needs. Volume that fails checks isn't volume.

steps.h: Fake and incentivised leads are fraud
steps.p: Some practices are not grey areas. They break network terms and, in many places, the law, and they hurt real people whose details are misused. No payout makes them acceptable.

d.text: Never generate, buy or recycle leads, never pay or reward people to apply, never submit data on someone's behalf, and never resell a lead beyond its consent. Expect clawbacks, bans and possible legal action.

steps.h: Starting rules for lead quality
steps.p: Starting rules to adapt. Check them daily during a test, then weekly once a source is stable. Each one tells you exactly what to do, so you are not guessing under pressure.

Pause when duplicates exceed 10% of leads
Investigate when median fill time is under 15 seconds
Exclude any placement scrubbing 2 x your average
Resume only after a fix and a small test of 30+ leads

Investigate when median fill time is under fifteen seconds. Exclude any placement scrubbing two times your average. And resume only after a fix and a small test of thirty or more leads. Check them daily during a test, then weekly once a source is stable.

steps.p: Your scrub rate turns gross leads into paid leads. Track it per source and per placement, not just per offer. In the worked example 22% scrub plus 6% returns left a margin of about 2.5%.

Scrubs and returns can turn a profitable-looking CPL into a loss.
Fake, incentivised or resold leads are fraud, not a growth tactic.

lessons.title: Loans, cards, insurance and banking compared
objectives: By the end you can match each finance product to the person it fits and the harm it can cause.
You can compare products on revenue for the same spend.
You can name the loan offers you should refuse to promote.
You can choose a sensible first product for your budget.

steps.h: Why the product decides your whole campaign
steps.p: A loan, a card, an insurance policy and a bank account attract different people, pay on different events and fail in different ways. The product decides your angle, your disclosure, your cash cycle and how much harm a careless ad can do.

d.s: Angle, disclosure, cash cycle and risk all change with it.

steps.say: A loan, a card, an insurance policy and a bank account attract different people, pay on different events, and fail in different ways. So the product decides your angle, your disclosure, your cash cycle, and how much harm a careless ad can do. As the slide says: different product, different rules.

steps.h: Who each product fits and what to show
steps.p: Rough guide. Disclosure rules are set per country and per product. Ask the advertiser for the exact wording for your geo, and never shorten it to fit a design.

rows: Has a planned cost and steady income
Has a brief gap and can repay fast
Wants flexible credit and pays on time
Needs cover for a real risk
Insurer, what is and is not covered
Wants to save, pay or receive money

steps.say: This table shows who each product fits, and what you must typically show. A personal loan fits someone with a planned cost and steady income; show the rate, total repayable and term. A short-term loan fits a brief gap with fast repayment; show the full cost, and expect strict rules. A credit card fits someone who pays on time; show rate, fees and eligibility. Insurance fits a real risk; name the insurer and what is and isn't covered. A bank account: show fees, dated rates and protection. Ask the advertiser for exact wording for your geo, and never shorten it to fit a design.

steps.h: Worked example: the same $500 on four products
steps.p: Example, illustrative rates. 1,250 clicks at $0.40 each on four different offers. Results are close, which is why value per click matters more than which product sounds most profitable.
steps.more: Check: 1,250 x $0.40 = $500 spend in each row. Loan: 1,250 x 1.2% = 15 x $40 = $600. Card: 1,250 x 0.8% = 10 x $55 = $550. Insurance: 1,250 x 6% = 75 x $7 = $525. Bank: 1,250 x 4% = 50 x $12 = $600. The bank offer matches the loan offer with far less harm risk and usually a faster confirmation.

The loan, at forty dollars funded, makes six hundred, a hundred profit. The card, at fifty five approved, makes fifty profit. Insurance, at seven dollars a quote, makes twenty five. And the bank account, at twelve dollars opened, also makes a hundred. The results are close. That's why value per click matters more than which product sounds most profitable. And the bank offer matches the loan with far less harm risk, and usually faster confirmation.

steps.h: Example: how long until the paid event confirms
steps.p: Example, rough guide, varies widely by advertiser. Faster confirmation means you learn faster and need less cash to wait. For your first offer, speed of learning is worth a lot.
steps.say: These bars show how long each paid event takes to confirm, as a rough example that varies widely. An insurance quote lead, about seven days. A bank account opened, about fourteen. A card approved, about twenty one. A loan funded, about thirty days. Faster confirmation means you learn faster, and need less cash to wait. For your first offer, that speed of learning is worth a lot.

steps.h: Some loan offers should never be promoted
steps.p: Predatory lending exists. It means lending designed to profit from people who cannot afford it: hidden fees, endless rollovers, abusive collection, misuse of phone contacts. A high payout on such an offer is paid for by the borrower's harm, and it puts your accounts at risk.
steps.more: Signs we cover in depth in module 2: the lender is not on the regulator's list; the cost is not shown before applying; fees are deducted upfront so the borrower receives less than advertised; repayment terms are days long with rollovers; the app asks for access to contacts or photos; reviews describe shaming calls to family or employers. In Nigeria and Kenya, regulators have acted against digital lenders over practices like these. If you see these signs, do not run the offer and tell your network why.

d.s: No payout is worth building someone else's debt trap.

steps.say: Some loan offers should never be promoted. Predatory lending means lending designed to profit from people who can't afford it: hidden fees, endless rollovers, abusive collection, and misuse of phone contacts. Warning signs include a lender not on the regulator's list, cost not shown before applying, fees taken upfront, and apps asking for contacts or photos. In Nigeria and Kenya, regulators have acted against digital lenders over practices like these. A high payout on such an offer is paid for by the borrower's harm. Refuse it, and tell your network why.

steps.h: Worked example: how a rollover grows a debt
steps.p: Example. A 30-day loan of KES 10,000 with a KES 1,500 fee. The borrower cannot repay, pays only the fee and rolls over three times. After four months they have paid KES 6,000 in fees and still owe the KES 10,000.
steps.more: Check: 1,500 x 4 = 6,000. The borrower has paid 60% of the amount borrowed in fees and owes the full original amount. Some markets cap fees or limit rollovers; others do not. When you promote a loan, the ad that brought this person in is part of that story, which is why disclosure and targeting matter so much.
steps.say: Here's how a rollover grows a debt. A thirty day loan of ten thousand Kenyan shillings, with a fifteen hundred shilling fee. The borrower can't repay, so they pay only the fee and roll over, three times. Read the sum on screen. Fifteen hundred times four periods equals six thousand shillings paid, and the debt is unchanged. That's sixty percent of the amount borrowed, paid in fees, while still owing all of it. When you promote a loan, the ad that brought this person in is part of that story.

steps.h: Insurance: what changes
steps.p: Insurance leads are often easier on the user than loans, but they bring their own rules. Promises about cover are where most problems start, because a person finds out the truth only when they claim.

Cover, not price alone|What is and is not covered
No unproven cheapest claims|Only if the advertiser can prove it
Renewal timing|Car and device cover renew yearly

Choosing on payout size

steps.h: Starting rules for your first finance product
steps.p: Starting rules to adapt. They favour fast learning and low harm while you build skill. Relax them only once you have three matured, profitable tests behind you.
steps.more: Example: expected CPC $0.40. Value per click must be at least $0.52. The loan offer in the worked example has $40 x 1.2% = $0.48 per click, so it fails this rule. The bank offer has $12 x 4% = $0.48 too and also fails; you would need a better rate or a lower CPC before starting.
d: Pick a paid event that confirms within 14 days
Avoid short-term and high-cost loans as a first offer
Value per click must be ≥ 1.3 x your expected CPC
Licence verified and disclosure wording received
Refuse any offer showing a predatory red flag
steps.say: Here are your starting rules for a first finance product. Pick a paid event that confirms within fourteen days. Avoid short-term and high cost loans as a first offer. Value per click must be at least one point three times your expected C P C, cost per click. Have the licence verified and disclosure wording received. And refuse any offer showing a predatory red flag. For example, with a forty cent C P C, you need at least fifty two cents per click, so both the loan and bank offers at forty eight cents would fail. Relax these only after three matured, profitable tests.

steps.h: Why the offer page is a contract
steps.p: The offer page tells you what you will be paid for, what traffic is allowed and what gets you banned. Most disputes in finance come from a line someone did not read. Ten minutes of reading saves weeks of unpaid leads.

d.b: Read every line before you spend
d.s: Most unpaid leads trace back to a rule nobody read.

steps.say: The offer page tells you what you'll be paid for, what traffic is allowed, and what gets you banned. Most disputes in finance come from a line someone didn't read. As the slide says: read every line before you spend. Ten minutes of reading saves weeks of unpaid leads.

steps.h: A finance offer page, line by line
steps.p: The payout definition is the line to read first. Then the traffic rules, then the hold and payment terms, then the cap. Screen is an illustrative mock-up; real offer pages differ by network.

blocks.label: Allowed traffic
blocks.value: Social (special ad category required), search, email with consent

blocks.label: Not allowed
blocks.value: Incentivised, brand bidding, guaranteed approval claims

steps.say: Here's a finance offer page, as an illustrative mock-up. Read the highlighted payout line first: thirty eight dollars per disbursed loan. Then the traffic rules: social with a special ad category, search, and email with consent. Not allowed: incentivised traffic, brand bidding, and guaranteed approval claims. Then hold and payment: a thirty day hold, paid net fifteen. And finally the cap, sixty disbursed loans a day. That's the order to read in.

steps.h: Questions to ask before you spend
steps.p: Ask in writing and keep the replies in your offer file. If a manager cannot answer one, treat it as a no until they can.
steps.say: Here are the questions to ask before you spend, with why each matters. The exact paid event, because approval and funding differ. The funded rate for social traffic, which sets your max C P L, cost per lead. The approval window, which sets when you judge. A postback for each status, so you can see cohorts. The licence and legal entity, which you must verify. The required cost disclosure, for your ad and page. And the consent wording for forms. Ask in writing. If a manager can't answer one, treat it as a no until they can.

steps.h: Use network EPC with care
steps.p: Networks often show EPC, earnings per click from all affiliates. It is a hint, not a promise, because other affiliates' traffic is not yours. Example: EPC $0.45, your expected CPC $0.38.
steps.more: Example. A $0.07 margin on a $0.38 click is about 18% before scrubs, returns and lag. That is thin. EPC from search or email traffic can be much higher than what social traffic earns on the same offer, so ask which sources make up the number. Plan with a cautious rate, then switch to your own data.
steps.say: Networks often show E P C, earnings per click, averaged across all affiliates. It's a hint, not a promise, because other affiliates' traffic isn't yours. Read the example sum. An E P C of forty five cents, minus your expected C P C, cost per click, of thirty eight cents, leaves a seven cent margin per click. That's about eighteen percent, before scrubs, returns and lag. Thin. E P C from search or email can be much higher than social on the same offer, so ask which sources make up the number.

steps.h: Worked example: two offers side by side
steps.p: Example. Offer A pays more per lead but slowly. Offer B pays less but fast. With $600 of spare cash, B is the better first offer even though A wins on paper.
steps.more: Example maths. A: $60 x 0.06 = $3.60. B: $3.20 x 0.9 = $2.88. A is worth 1.25 x more per lead. But at $100 a day, A needs roughly six weeks of spend, $4,200, before the first payout arrives. With $600 of spare cash you cannot run A properly, so B is the honest choice for now.

exam.q: Offer pays $30 per approval. Your leads cost $3 and 8% are approved. What is your profit or loss per lead?
You spent $120 on a loan offer. Target cost per approval is $25. The cohort is 3 days old with 1 approval and a 21-day window. What do you do?
options: Hold: the cohort is immature; check valid and application rates
exam.why: With lag, a 3-day cohort cannot be judged on cost per approval. Use leading signals until the window passes.

exam.q: CPL offer $4 with 25% scrub versus CPA $35 at 10% approval. Your cash buffer is two weeks. Which do you start with and why?
options: CPL, because the CPA's edge is under 1.2 x and cash is short
exam.why: CPL = $3.00, CPA = $3.50 per lead. 3.50 / 3.00 = 1.17, under the 1.2 x rule, and cash is short.

exam.q: Your scrub rate jumps to 30% for two days, mostly invalid phones from one placement. What is the right sequence?
options: Exclude the placement, add phone verification, test 30+ leads before resuming
Ask the network to pay anyway
exam.why: Fix the cause, verify the fix with a small test, then resume.

exam.q: A new loan app pays $70 per funded loan, asks users for contact access and has reviews about calls to employers. What do you do?
options: Refuse it and tell the network why
Run it at a small budget
exam.why: Contact harvesting and shaming collection are predatory red flags. No copy fixes the product.

exam.q: 400 leads, 20% scrubbed, $3.50 per accepted lead, then 5% of accepted leads returned. Revenue?
Angle A: $2 per lead, 10% approved. Angle B: $3.20 per lead, 20% approved. Payout $30 per approval. Which angle do you keep?
options: B: $2.80 profit per lead against A's $1.00

exam.q: Two matured cohorts show $17 and $18 per approval with 6 and 7 approvals. Target is $24. What does the starting rule say?
options: Scale +20%: both ≤ 0.8 x target ($19.20) with ≥ 5 approvals
exam.why: 0.8 x $24 = $19.20. Both cohorts are under it with at least five approvals.
